headline: Rips Report Card: Blues A-, Bass D, Weakfish Finally Cashing the Check
subhead: The rip line off the Point is still moving water, but it's bluefish and weakfish paying the bills while bass have gone into hiding until dark.
body_markdown:
If I had to grade this week on the water, here's the card: bluefish get an A-minus, weakfish are climbing toward a B, fluke is a C that needed a location change to pass, striped bass is a flat D during daylight, and black drum — that class is over, kid, go home. That's where we're at heading into August.

The rips off Cape May Point are still doing their job current-wise. That color line between the Delaware Bay outflow and the green ocean water is showing up sharp on the back half of the ebb, and the bait is there — peanut bunker getting pushed and balled up right on the seam. But the bass that used to camp under that bait all day have wised up to the warm water. Surface temps sitting in the upper 70s pushed them off the shallow structure and out to the reef sites — Cape May Reef, Wildwood Reef, the edges out toward the Old Grounds — where they've gone almost strictly nocturnal. If you want a bass right now, you're fishing the last two hours of dark into first light, live-lining bunker or working an eel slow along bottom on the turn of the tide. Daytime trolling through the rips for bass has been mostly a bluefish tax this week — you'll get bit, just not by what you're targeting.

And that bluefish tax isn't a bad consolation prize. Blues have been the one species actually thriving in this warm water mass, and the rips have had a steady pull of 2- to 5-pound choppers on diamond jigs and green-tube Ava 27s, worked through the rip on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current's really cranking against the shoal. Bunker spoons trolled at 3 to 4 knots through the same water have been just as productive if you don't want to jig. It's not a blitz every trip, but it's a dependable bend in the rod, and worth the gas if bass aren't cooperating.

Fluke's been the tell of the summer. We flagged this last week — said the bay bite would soften as the shallows warmed and the better play would shift to deeper reef structure and the mouth of the bay, and that's exactly how it's played out. Inside the back bays and up around Hereford Inlet, the fluke bite has gone quiet and picky, mostly shorts. Move out to Wildwood Reef or Cape May Reef in 40 to 55 feet, though, and there's still a real bite going — 5-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the moving tide, mixing keepers with the shorts. It's not a beach-bum program anymore; you need to run out to structure to find fish willing to eat.

Weakfish are the other call that's playing out — we said last week to expect that bite to keep climbing as the water held steady, and it has. Delaware Bay's channel edges near Miah Maull Shoal and around Brandywine Shoal Light have been holding weakfish in 20 to 30 feet, and the last two hours of the incoming tide has been the window. Pink or chartreuse soft-plastic shad bodies on light jig heads, or straight bloodworms on a simple bottom rig, have both been drawing bites. Nothing like the old-timer weakfish runs my father used to talk about, but for the current state of that fishery, a mixed bag of keeper-class fish two or three days a week is a genuinely good sign.

As for black drum — that ship sailed in May and it's not coming back this year. Fortescue's quiet on that front, just the odd straggler getting picked up incidentally by guys soaking clam for something else. If you're still asking about drum, you missed the window; start planning for next May instead.

One more thing worth a mention if you're bottom fishing the reef sites: triggerfish have been showing up as a bonus on clam baits fished tight to structure on Cape May Reef. Not a target species most guys plan a trip around, but a fun surprise when the fluke bite goes cold on the drift.

Looking ahead, the tides are easing off the post-full-moon push and sliding toward neap over the next several days, which usually means a little less current speed through the rips and a slightly calmer bite window overall. That's fine for weakfish and fluke, who don't need violent water to feed, but it typically softens the bluefish blitz pattern some as bait disperses with the slacker current. By the back half of next week, we'll be building tide again toward the August 12 new moon, and that's when I'd expect the rips to sharpen back up and bass activity — even at night — to get a little more aggressive around the bait balls. If the warm surface layer holds like it has, don't expect striped bass to come back to a daytime program anytime soon. Plan your trips around dark, fish the reef structure for fluke, and work the bay's channel edges for weakfish on the incoming. That's the honest version of this week, no sugarcoating it.
